subproblems.title: Uniform bound and Lipschitz bound for D^2 Psi on a closed ball of L(R^n, R^l)
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, L := L(R^n, R^l) (continuous linear maps Rn n ->L Rn l with the operator norm), Psi : L -> R of class C^3 and eps a real number. Write B(P)[Q][Q'] := D^2 Psi(P)[Q][Q'] = fderiv R (fderiv R Psi) P Q Q'. Then there are real numbers M_B >= 0 and L_B >= 0 such that (i) |B(P)[Q][Q']| <= M_B ||Q|| ||Q'|| for all P, Q, Q' in L with ||P|| <= eps, and (ii) |B(P)[Q][Q'] - B(P')[Q][Q']| <= L_B ||P - P'|| ||Q|| ||Q'|| for all P, P', Q, Q' in L with ||P|| <= eps and ||P'|| <= eps.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (Ψ : (Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ) → ℝ), ContDiff ℝ 3 Ψ → ∀ ε : ℝ, ∃ MB LB : ℝ, 0 ≤ MB ∧ 0 ≤ LB ∧ (∀ P : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ, ‖P‖ ≤ ε → ∀ Q Q' : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ, |fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ Ψ) P Q Q'| ≤ MB * ‖Q‖ * ‖Q'‖) ∧ ∀ P P' : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ, ‖P‖ ≤ ε → ‖P'‖ ≤ ε → ∀ Q Q' : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ, |fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ Ψ) P Q Q' - fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ Ψ) P' Q Q'| ≤ LB * ‖P - P'‖ * ‖Q‖ * ‖Q'‖
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Step 1 of the parent proof (the constants M_B, L_B of Psi on the closed eps-ball), written out in full.
Notation. L is a finite-dimensional real normed space, so its closed balls are compact. Let L* := L(L, R) and Bil := L(L, L*) be the spaces of continuous linear forms and of continuous bilinear forms on L with their operator norms; for beta in Bil and Q, Q' in L, |beta[Q][Q']| <= ||beta[Q]|| ||Q'|| <= ||beta|| ||Q|| ||Q'|| (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm2). Put A := D Psi : L -> L* and B := D A : L -> Bil, so that B(P)[Q][Q'] = fderiv R (fderiv R Psi) P Q Q'.
1. Regularity. Psi is C^3, hence A = fderiv R Psi is C^2 and B = fderiv R A is C^1 (ContDiff.fderiv_right, twice). So B is continuous, B is differentiable at every point, and its derivative DB = fderiv R B : L -> L(L, Bil) is continuous (ContDiff.continuous_fderiv).
2. The set Kc := closedBall(0, eps) in L is compact (finite dimension; for eps < 0 it is empty, which is also compact) and convex.

1. Continuity in t. Psi is C^2, so A := fderiv R Psi is C^1 and B = fderiv R A : L -> Bil is continuous (ContDiff.fderiv_right, ContDiff.continuous_fderiv). For fixed x, P, Q the maps t -> B(P_t(x))[P] in L* and t -> B(P_t(x))[P][Q] in R are continuous (t -> P_t(x) is affine, evaluation maps are continuous linear), hence interval integrable on [0,1].
2. Construction of a and the formula. Fix x. Define l_x : L -> L* by l_x(P) := integral_0^1 B(P_t(x))[P] dt. It is linear: B(P_t(x)) is linear, so the integrand for P + P' (resp. cP) is the sum (resp. c times) of the integrands, and the interval integral is additive and homogeneous on interval-integrable functions (step 1; intervalIntegral.integral_add, intervalIntegral.integral_smul). L is finite-dimensional, so the linear map l_x is continuous; let a(x) in L(L, L*) be l_x as a continuous linear map (LinearMap.toContinuousLinearMap). Evaluation at Q is a continuous linear map L* -> R and commutes with the integral of the integrable integrand (ContinuousLinearMap.intervalIntegral_apply), so a(x)[P][Q] = (integral_0^1 B(P_t(x))[P] dt)[Q] = integral_0^1 B(P_t(x))[P][Q] dt for every x in R^n and P, Q in L.
3. The segment stays in the ball. For x in S and t in [0,1]: ||P_t(x)|| <= (1 - t)||P0(x)|| + t||P1(x)|| <= (1 - t)eps + t eps = eps.
4. Coercivity. Let x in S and P in L. By step 3 and (a), B(P_t(x))[P][P] >= lam ||P||^2 for every t in [0,1]. Both sides are integrable on [0,1] (step 1), so by monotonicity of the interval integral (intervalIntegral.integral_mono_on) and step 2, a(x)[P][P] = integral_0^1 B(P_t(x))[P][P] dt >= integral_0^1 lam ||P||^2 dt = lam ||P||^2.
5. Bound. Let x in S and P, Q in L. For t in (0,1], |B(P_t(x))[P][Q]| <= M_B ||P|| ||Q|| by step 3 and (b). By step 2 and the estimate of an interval integral by a constant (intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const), |a(x)[P][Q]| <= M_B ||P|| ||Q|| |1 - 0| = M_B ||P|| ||Q||.
6. Hoelder continuity. Let x, y in S, P, Q in L and t in [0,1]. P_t(x) - P_t(y) = (1 - t)(P0(x) - P0(y)) + t(P1(x) - P1(y)), so ||P_t(x) - P_t(y)|| <= (1 - t)H||x - y||^alpha + tH||x - y||^alpha = H||x - y||^alpha (a convex combination of the two hypotheses; no sign condition on H is needed). Lebesgue measure on R^n is translation invariant: integral F(y + c) dy = integral F(y) dy for every F and every c (integral_add_right_eq_self; no integrability is needed). zeta and Dzeta are continuous, zeta(y) = 0 and Dzeta(y) = 0 for y not in K (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), and g is continuous at every point of U (U is open). Let c(s) := max(0, min(s, 1)) be the clamp of s to [0,1]: c is continuous, c(s) lies in [0,1], and c(s) = s for s in [0,1]. Write G(y) := integral_0^1 g(y + (td)e) dt.
1. Difference formula. Fix x. k(s) := zeta(x - (sd)e) has derivative k'(s) = Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[-(de)] = -d Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[e] (chain rule), continuous in s. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt), zeta(x - de) - zeta(x) = k(1) - k(0) = -d integral_0^1 Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[e] ds, i.e. zeta(x) - zeta(x - de) = d integral_0^1 Dzeta(x - (sd)e)[e] ds.
2. Put F(s, x) := <Dzeta(x - (c(s)d)e)[e], g(x)>. By step 1, <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> = d * integral_0^1 F(s, x) ds for every x: pull d out of the inner product; on [0,1] one has c(s) = s (intervalIntegral.integral_congr); the continuous linear form v -> <g(x), v> commutes with the interval integral of the continuous integrand (ContinuousLinearMap.intervalIntegral_comp_comm with innerSL); the real inner product is symmetric.
3. F is continuous on R x R^n. Let (s, x) be given. If x - (c(s)d)e is not in K, then, K being closed and (s', x') -> x' - (c(s')d)e continuous, Dzeta vanishes at x' - (c(s')d)e for (s', x') near (s, x), so F = 0 near (s, x). If x - (c(s)d)e is in K, then x = (x - (c(s)d)e) + (c(s)d)e lies in U (hypothesis with t = c(s)), so g is continuous at x and F, an inner product of functions continuous at (s, x), is continuous at (s, x).
4. Integrability of F. F(s, x) = 0 whenever x is not in K' (if x - (c(s)d)e were in K, x would lie in K'). F is continuous, so it is integrable on the compact set [0,1] x K' for the product of Lebesgue measures (ContinuousOn.integrableOn_compact), hence on [0,1] x R^n since it vanishes on the rest (IntegrableOn.of_forall_sdiff_eq_zero), hence on (0,1] x R^n. Since (Lebesgue restricted to (0,1]) x Lebesgue = (Lebesgue x Lebesgue) restricted to (0,1] x R^n (Measure.prod_restrict), F is integrable for the measure used by Fubini's theorem for interval integrals.
5. Let Ft(s, y) := <Dzeta(y)[e], g(y + (c(s)d)e)>. If y is not in K, Ft vanishes near (s, y) (K closed); if y is in K, y + (c(s)d)e lies in U and g is continuous there. So Ft is continuous, vanishes outside R x K, and exactly as in step 4 it is integrable on (0,1] x R^n.
6. Translation. For each s, by translation invariance with x = y + (c(s)d)e: integral F(s, x) dx = integral F(s, y + (c(s)d)e) dy = integral Ft(s, y) dy.
7. Inner integral of Ft. For y in K the map s -> g(y + (sd)e) is continuous on [0,1] (the segment lies in U), hence interval integrable, and integral_0^1 Ft(s, y) ds = integral_0^1 <Dzeta(y)[e], g(y + (sd)e)> ds = <Dzeta(y)[e], G(y)> = <G(y), Dzeta(y)e> (c(s) = s on [0,1]; innerSL commutes with the integral; symmetry). For y not in K both sides are 0 because Dzeta(y) = 0.
8. Chain. integral <zeta(x) - zeta(x - de), g(x)> dx = integral d * (integral_0^1 F(s, x) ds) dx [step 2] = d * integral (integral_0^1 F(s, x) ds) dx [integral_const_mul] = d * integral_0^1 (integral F(s, x) dx) ds [Fubini, intervalIntegral_integral_swap with step 4] = d * integral_0^1 (integral Ft(s, y) dy) ds [step 6] = d * integral (integral_0^1 Ft(s, y) ds) dy [Fubini with step 5] = d * integral <G(y), Dzeta(y)e> dy [step 7]. QED

Source: Step 3 and Step 5 (H5)-(H7) of the parent proof.
1. For x in V the whole segment {x + (td)e : t in [0,1]} lies in K, a subset of U; in particular x (t = 0) and x + de (t = 1) lie in K. Since U is open and u is C^1 on U, u is differentiable at every point of U.
2. (i) The translation z -> z + de is smooth and maps V into U (step 1), so z -> u(z + de) is C^1 on V (ContDiffOn.comp); u is C^1 on V, a subset of U (ContDiffOn.mono). Hence w = d^{-1}(u(. + de) - u) is C^1 on V.
3. (ii) Fix x in V. u is differentiable at x + de, so z -> u(z + de) has derivative Du(x + de) at x (chain rule with the translation); u has derivative Du(x) at x. By linearity of the derivative, w has derivative d^{-1}(Du(x + de) - Du(x)) at x, so Dw(x) = d^{-1}(Du(x + de) - Du(x)).
4. (iii) Fix x in V and let h(t) := u(x + (td)e). For t in [0,1], x + (td)e lies in K, a subset of U, so h has derivative h'(t) = Du(x + (td)e)[de] with ||h'(t)|| <= ||Du(x + (td)e)|| ||de|| <= eps |d| ||e|| (multiplying ||Du|| <= eps by ||de|| >= 0). By the mean value inequality on [0,1] (norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_deriv_le_segment_01'), ||u(x + de) - u(x)|| = ||h(1) - h(0)|| <= eps |d| ||e||. Hence ||w(x)|| = |d|^{-1} ||u(x + de) - u(x)|| <= |d|^{-1} eps |d| ||e|| = eps ||e|| (d nonzero).
5. (iv) For x, y in V, by (ii): Dw(x) - Dw(y) = d^{-1}[(Du(x + de) - Du(y + de)) - (Du(x) - Du(y))]. The four points x, y, x + de, y + de lie in K (step 1) and (x + de) - (y + de) = x - y, so ||Dw(x) - Dw(y)|| <= |d|^{-1}(H||x - y||^alpha + H||x - y||^alpha) = 2|d|^{-1} H ||x - y||^alpha. QED

1. C^1 on U. Every x in U has the open neighbourhood B_r(x) on which f is C^1, so f is C^1 on U intersected with B_r(x). By the local characterization of ContDiffOn (contDiffOn_of_locally_contDiffOn), f is C^1 on U.
2. Norm identity. For all x, y: ||iteratedFDeriv R 1 f x - iteratedFDeriv R 1 f y|| = ||Df(x) - Df(y)||. Indeed continuousMultilinearCurryFin1 is a linear isometric equivalence from (R^n [x1]->L R^l) to L(R^n, R^l) sending iteratedFDeriv R 1 f z to Df(z) for every z (iteratedFDeriv_one_apply), so it maps the difference to the difference and preserves norms. It therefore suffices to bound ||Df(x) - Df(y)|| on compact sets.
3. Fix a compact K contained in U. Since U is open and f is C^1 on U, Df is continuous on U (ContDiffOn.continuousOn_fderiv_of_isOpen), hence bounded on K: there is B with ||Df(y)|| <= B for y in K; put B' := max(B, 0).
4. Finite subcover. For each x in K choose r_x > 0 and C_x as in the hypothesis. The open balls B_{r_x}(x), x in K, cover K; by compactness finitely many of them, B_{r_i}(x_i) for i in a finite set T, cover K (IsCompact.elim_finite_subcover). Put C* := sum over i in T of |C_i|; then C* >= 0 and C* >= C_i for all i in T.
5. Lebesgue number. By lebesgue_number_lemma_of_metric applied to the finite open cover of the compact K, there is delta > 0 such that for every y in K there is i in T with B_delta(y) contained in B_{r_i}(x_i).
6. Let C' := C* + 2B'/delta^alpha. Let y, z in K.
 (a) If ||y - z|| < delta: choose i with B_delta(y) contained in B_{r_i}(x_i). Then y and z lie in B_{r_i}(x_i), so ||Df(y) - Df(z)|| <= C_i ||y - z||^alpha <= C* ||y - z||^alpha <= C' ||y - z||^alpha (using ||y - z||^alpha >= 0 and 2B'/delta^alpha >= 0).
 (b) If ||y - z|| >= delta: then delta^alpha <= ||y - z||^alpha (alpha > 0), and ||Df(y) - Df(z)|| <= ||Df(y)|| + ||Df(z)|| <= 2B' = (2B'/delta^alpha) delta^alpha <= (2B'/delta^alpha) ||y - z||^alpha <= C' ||y - z||^alpha.
